"Outgoing" has two separate meanings as an adjective, and they are quite different from each other. You need to know both to truly understand this word.

This is the most common and important meaning. When you describe a person as outgoing, you mean they are naturally comfortable and enthusiastic around other people. They enjoy socializing, meeting strangers, starting conversations, and being part of a group. Being around others gives them energy rather than draining them.

An outgoing person:

  • walks into a room full of strangers and starts talking without hesitation
  • makes friends easily and quickly
  • is warm, cheerful, and approachable
  • enjoys parties, social gatherings, and group activities
  • speaks up confidently in conversations

This is a personality trait — something stable about how a person is, not just how they behave on one particular day.

Examples:

  • "She is so outgoing — she introduced herself to everyone at the party within minutes."
  • "He's very outgoing, which makes him excellent at his job as a salesperson."
  • "Even as a child, Maya was outgoing and never afraid to raise her hand in class."

What "outgoing" does NOT mean here

Being outgoing does not mean being loud, rude, or overbearing. An outgoing person can be perfectly polite and respectful — they are simply at ease with social interaction. It also doesn't mean they have no depth or are shallow. Many thoughtful, intelligent people are outgoing.

It also does not mean the same as being extroverted in the clinical, psychological sense, though the two words are very closely related and are often used interchangeably in everyday speech. In casual use, saying someone is "outgoing" or "extroverted" usually means the same thing.

The scale of outgoing-ness

"Outgoing" is not all-or-nothing. People can be:

  • Very outgoing — the life of the party, loves being the center of attention
  • Fairly outgoing — comfortable in social situations but doesn't need to be the loudest person in the room
  • Somewhat outgoing — can socialize well when needed but doesn't actively seek it out

Synonyms and how they differ

  • Sociable — very similar; means enjoying the company of others. Perhaps slightly softer than "outgoing." An outgoing person is always sociable, but a sociable person isn't always as bold or as energetic about it as an outgoing person.
  • Extroverted — nearly identical in everyday use. In psychology, an extrovert is someone who gains energy from social interaction.
  • Friendly — this just means being warm and pleasant toward others. A friendly person might still be shy or reserved. Outgoing goes further — it also implies actively seeking social connection.
  • Gregarious — very similar to outgoing, but slightly more formal. It specifically emphasizes enjoying group settings and the company of many people.
  • Confident — being outgoing usually involves confidence, but confidence is broader (you can be confident about many things). An outgoing person has social confidence specifically.

Antonym

The opposite of outgoing (in this sense) is introverted, reserved, shy, or withdrawn.

  • Shy — feels nervous, uncomfortable, or self-conscious around others
  • Reserved — not shy necessarily, but keeps to themselves, doesn't open up easily
  • Introverted — prefers less social stimulation; socializing feels draining rather than energizing
Meaning 2: Leaving, Departing, or Going Out

This is the second meaning, used in very specific, mostly formal or official contexts. Here, "outgoing" simply means something that is in the process of leaving or going out, as opposed to coming in.

Examples:

  • "The outgoing president" — the president who is currently finishing their term and about to leave the position (as opposed to the incoming president who is just taking over)
  • "Outgoing mail" — letters or packages being sent out from an office (as opposed to incoming mail, which is being received)
  • "The outgoing tide" — the tide that is currently moving away from the shore (as opposed to the incoming tide)
  • "The outgoing flight" — a flight that is departing (especially when seen from the perspective of the place it's leaving)

Notice that in this meaning, "outgoing" is almost always paired with a noun — it describes that noun as "going out" or "leaving." This meaning is fairly straightforward and you will almost always understand it from the context.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Context will always make it clear:

  • If "outgoing" describes a person's character or personality, it means sociable and friendly.
  • If "outgoing" describes a position, a message, a tide, or something leaving, it means departing or going out.

You will almost never confuse the two in real life.
A Note on Register and Usage

In its personality sense, "outgoing" is a positive and complimentary word. Calling someone outgoing is generally a compliment — it suggests they are easy to be around and fun in social settings. It is used equally in casual conversation and professional writing. You might see it on a resume ("I am an outgoing team player"), in a novel describing a character, or in everyday speech about someone you know.

In its departing sense, "outgoing" tends to appear in formal or institutional language — official documents, news articles, business communication, and so on. It is less common in casual, everyday speech.

Outgoing (about a person): Naturally sociable, friendly, comfortable meeting new people, and energized by social interaction.

Outgoing (about things/positions): Currently leaving, being sent out, or in the final phase before being replaced — the opposite of "incoming."
